newsitem.title: SPAIN: FORECAST - Spain's six-mth bills seen resuming fall.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Spain's six-mth bills seen resuming fall.

text.p: Yields of Spanish six-month bills are expected to fall at auction on Wednesday for the first time since mid-February, dealers said on Tuesday.
Expectations for a decline in March CPI and improved optimism over European single currency prospects has pushed yields for six-month bills trading on the grey-market down.
Grey-market bills are yielding 5.43 percent, down from 5.573 percent, the marginal yield at the latest auction on March 25.

"The auction tomorrow of six-month bills is not attracting much interest. But there's no doubt, given the fall in money market rates, that their marginal rate will fall," a money market dealer in Madrid said.
In recent days, money market rates fell sharply, while the peseta bounced back versus the mark amid fresh expectations of imminent, further official rate cuts.
March CPI, seen falling to below 2.4 percent year-on-year after a 2.5 rise in February is also considered as a factor.
Analysts said tame data could prompt the Bank of Spain to sanction its third official rate cut this year.
The Bank of Spain last cut 25 percentage points of its key rate on March 14. The rate now stands at 5.75 percent.
Prices of MIBOR short-term futures contracts, which had been stable in recent weeks, have been rising since April 2.
"The market is reviewing expectations, awaiting March CPI on Friday, and pricing in a possible official rate cut," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
"The three-month MIBOR September future recovered by 35 basis points in the last two days," said Urrutia.
Since April 2, the one-year MIBOR has fallen by 0.25 basis points.

"In a couple of weeks, the market has changed its short-term perspective completely. Before no-one wanted to touch one-year bills yielding 5.57 percent and Spain's Treasury had to rise their yield to 5.59 at the auction. Now there's no doubt a yield around 5.40 percent seems good," another dealer said.
Last weekend, EU finance ministers improved the market's mood by reducing fears of a possible delay to Europe's single currency.
"The confirmation of the start is supporting more the countries that suffered the most when doubts arose," said Valentin Fernandez, economist of Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
